Hungary moves to scrap Orban-era anti-LGBTQ+ ‘promotion’ rules

PM Peter Magyar’s government has submitted a bill removing restrictions on LGBTQ+ content for under-18s, following an EU court ruling that found the rules breached EU law

Reuters

15 September, 2026 04:40 pm IST

Facebook

File photo of a person attending the Budapest Pride march in Budapest | Photo: Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Hungary: Hungary’s government submitted a bill to parliament late on Monday that would remove anti-LGBTQ+ rules prohibiting the “promotion of homosexuality” to under-18s implemented by Viktor Orban’s former nationalist government.

Orban’s government, which was ousted after 16 years in an election in April, promoted a Christian-conservative agenda and in 2021 banned the “display and promotion of homosexuality” and gender change in media content accessible by under-18s.

Orban said the anti-LGBTQ+ laws were to protect children, but the restriuctions attracted strong criticism from rights groups and the European Union.

Show Full Article

Hungary’s new Justice Minister Marta Gorog said in May that Hungary would need to revise legislation restricting access to LGBTQ+ content after the EU’s top court ruled in April that the restrictions breached EU law and contributed to the stigmatisation and marginalisation of gay and transgender people.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who swept to power in April, has pledged to repair ties with the EU. Putting Hungary back into the EU’s mainstream also requires addressing concerns over democratic standards and minority rights.

The draft bill would ban materials that can “seriously impair the child’s physical, intellectual, emotional or moral development.”

“The proposal focuses on the actual dangers facing children. Protection centers on pornographic and age-inappropriate sexual content, the sexual exploitation and abuse of children, sexual solicitation and manipulation, as well as other content that severely harms children’s physical, intellectual, emotional, or moral development,” the legislation says.

Magyar said on Saturday that his government would also change rules that had effectively banned gay adoption

Sucked out of plane window? Ryanair CEO says passenger doesn’t deserve ‘millions and millions’

In July, 61-year-old Serbian businessman Ljubisa Karović was injured on a Ryanair flight from Greece to Germany. His wife said she had to hold him by his legs to prevent him from being sucked out.

Purvi Rajpuria

15 September, 2026 04:31 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Ultra-low-cost airline Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary has disputed the claim that any part of a passenger’s body was sucked out of the plane when one of its windows broke mid-flight in July this year, Good Morning America reported.

Dismissing the passenger’s allegations, O’Leary said, “We don’t think any part of his body got out the window, but he was certainly sucked in very dramatic circumstances towards the window.”

O’Leary also called the passenger’s wife “somewhat delusional” after she claimed to have held him by his legs to prevent him from being sucked out. He alleged that the wife was actually seated three rows behind her husband.

Show Full Article

O’Leary’s comments came last Thursday as he addressed reporters following Ryanair’s annual general meeting in Dublin. He said he would challenge the passenger’s account while awaiting the outcome of the US National Transportation Safety Board’s (NTSB) investigation into the incident.

While the CEO stressed that he was not trying to downplay the incident, he also said the passenger was entitled to “some compensation”, but not a multi-million-euro payout, ABC News reported .

The NTSB has criticised O’Leary for discussing the incident publicly while the investigation is still underway.

Serious neck and shoulder injuries The incident took place on 10 July, shortly after take-off, when passenger Ljubisa Karović alleged that he was lifted out of his seat, pulled into the plane’s airstream and hung headfirst out of the window. According to his legal team, Karović’s seatbelt prevented him from being sucked completely out of the aircraft.

The 61-year-old Serbian businessman suffered serious neck and shoulder injuries and was hospitalised. His wife later shared images of the shattered window and dangling oxygen masks from inside the plane.

The Ryanair Boeing 737-8AS, operated by the airline’s subsidiary Malta Air, was flying from Greece to Germany. An engine failure reportedly caused debris to shatter the plane’s acrylic window, resulting in sudden depressurisation.

The flight was then forced to make an emergency landing in Thessaloniki, from where it had taken off. Karović received medical attention on the ground soon after.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

US facing munitions shortage amid Iran offensive. Pentagon flags cost of war, resupply bottlenecks

DoD estimated it had spent $22.3 bn worth of expended munitions in the war as of about the end of June, while the overall cost through that period totaled more than $33 billion.

Tony Capaccio

15 September, 2026 03:53 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Men gather at the damage to the storage and warehousing facilities at the port of Kuhestak following a US military strike earlier in the week on Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, Iran. | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

The US fired so many munitions at Iranian targets during the first few months of Operation Epic Fury that it “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” Pentagon officials acknowledged to the Defence Department’s independent watchdog.

Acquisition officials said they are “working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times, and to stockpile critical materials, components, and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency,” the Pentagon inspector general said in a report released late Monday.

The IG report which covers the US military’s operations in the conflict with Iran through June 30, marks an official confirmation of a problem the Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed.

Show Full Article

“The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types,” Trump posted on social media Aug 6. In another post Sept. 9, Trump said the US has “virtually unlimited amounts” of mid- to high-grade ammunition — “far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War.”

The Defense Department estimated it had spent $22.3 billion worth of expended munitions in the war as of about the end of June, according to the report, while the overall cost through that period totaled more than $33 billion.

The report is the Pentagon IG’s first quarterly assessment of Operation Epic Fury, and reads as a high-level budgetary guide to the cost of the war, with dollar amounts attached. Congress requires these quarterly reports on US military operations where appropriated dollars are spent. The report includes contributions from the watchdogs overseeing the State Department and US Agency for International Development.

Iran’s military has damaged or destroyed “hundreds” of buildings and structures at US bases in the region, while US diplomatic facilities in four countries sustained physical damage from Iranian strikes, US Central Command told the IG.

The report listed 11 US service members killed in action as of the end of July, with another seven killed in non-hostile events during Epic Fury combat operations. More than 400 service members were wounded in action through the end of June.

The Pentagon didn’t release an immediate comment on the report.

NATO jets shoot down ‘unidentified’ drone that entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus

The drone was intercepted near Kruonis hydroelectric power plant. In previous months, similar incidents were also registered in Latvia and Estonia.

Milda Seputyte

15 September, 2026 01:57 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Italian Air Force Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets. Photographer: | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

NATO jets shot down an unidentified drone that flew into the Lithuanian airspace from neighboring Belarus early Tuesday, the latest incursion on the alliance’s eastern flank as aerial warfare between Ukraine and Russia intensifies.

The drone was intercepted over Pratkunai in central Lithuania, the area close to a hydroelectric power plant of Kruonis, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said. Air alerts sounded out over the capital region of Vilnius and the country’s second-largest city Kaunas before the drone was brought down.

It was the first time that NATO shot down a drone over the territory of Lithuania. The incident follows similar incidents in neighboring Latvia and Estonia in recent months. Intensifying exchanges of air attacks between Ukraine and Russia are turning into a growing issue for NATO countries as drones are jammed or veer off course.

Show Full Article

“Even though the war seems to be taking place a thousand kilometers away from Lithuania, its scale is still large and extensive,” Kaunas told national broadcaster LRT Tuesday. “Russia’s unwillingness to come to peace negotiations affects the security of the Baltic region.”

NATO jets downed a drone over Latvia in August after it entered the country’s airspace as a result of Russian electronic warfare, and a Romanian F-16 shot down a suspected Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May. Poland said Monday that the Polish military retrieved a Russian military UAV from the Baltic Sea near the town of Rusinowo.

European officials have also warned that Russia may escalate sabotage and covert attacks against the continent as it struggles to make progress in its war in Ukraine that’s now in a fifth year. Germany earlier this month attributed a drone attack on a Leipzig airport to Russian intelligence and said it expects further hybrid aggression.
